claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy has high strength but limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle behavior.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal colony boundaries cause local stress concentrations and microcracking in the starting alloy.
The proposed intervention is an addition of approximately 0.5–1 at.% boron during melting followed by annealing.
Annealing at approximately 600–700 °C for a short duration will encourage boron segregation to the lamellar interfaces.
Boron will preferentially segregate to dual-phase lamellar colony boundaries during controlled annealing.
Segregated boron will form thin, boron-enriched, complexion-like interfacial films at lamellar colony boundaries.
Boron segregation will lower the local boundary energy.
Boron-enriched interfacial films will increase interface compliance.
The modified interfaces will reduce the barrier to dislocation transmission across colony boundaries.
Improved dislocation transmission will reduce dislocation pile-ups and associated local stress concentrations.
Reduced dislocation pile-ups and stress concentrations will suppress premature microcrack initiation and catastrophic damage.
Solid-solution and possible minor precipitation effects will maintain or slightly enhance the alloy's strength.
Relative to the untreated alloy, boron addition and annealing may increase elongation to failure by more than 50% at room temperature.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the treatment will maintain or modestly increase yield strength.
The predicted benefits apply to room-temperature tensile testing at standard strain rates under laboratory ambient conditions.
Excess boron or overly aggressive annealing may form extensive brittle borides and cause embrittlement.
